title: Young or old?: There’s both
caption: The young star Ve 7-27 and the Vela Junior supernova remnant, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Energetic jets studded with knots, like bullets, shoot out of one object in this picture, while a compact yellowish-green smudge sits centre-left. The object with jets is Ve 7-27, which astronomers long believed was a planetary nebula, the final stage in the life of a star like the Sun. ESO's Very Large Telescope has shown it is actually a baby star still forming.

MUSE, an instrument on the VLT, captured the first detailed image of it. Jets with knots are typical of newborn stars. Lead author Janette Suherli described it as a newborn rather than a dying star's last breath.

A dead star is nearby too. The yellowish-green smudge hosts a neutron star left by a supernova, part of the Vela Junior remnant. The baby star is embedded in that supernova's debris, so the two are at the same distance. That finally pins down the remnant's size, expansion speed, energy and age.
scale: Ve 7-27, and therefore Vela Junior, is about 4500 light-years away, according to ESO.

understand.summary: The VLT's MUSE instrument imaged the region in visible light, using the emission of nickel, nitrogen and hydrogen-alpha. The colour mapping isn't published.
filters: 737 nm · Optical Nickel (Very Large Telescope MUSE)
658 nm · Optical Nitrogen (Very Large Telescope MUSE)
656 nm · Optical H-alpha (Very Large Telescope MUSE)
understand.eye: MUSE separates the light of individual elements, revealing jets and knots the eye could not distinguish.

explore: Suherli is a PhD candidate at the University of Manitoba in Canada. She describes the scene as a star being born right beside the remains of one that died, and the finding resolves decades of inconsistencies about Vela Junior.
alt: A young star shooting knotty jets, with a compact yellowish-green smudge to the centre-left.
